questions.q: What governance problem existed before Unity Catalog?
options: Permissions, audit logs, and lineage were set per workspace, with no single answer to who could see a table anywhere
Databricks had no permission system of any kind
Tables could only be queried with Python, never SQL
Workspaces could not connect to cloud storage at all
questions.explain: Before Unity Catalog, governance was workspace-by-workspace; Unity Catalog centralizes it on one metastore so a grant applies everywhere the object is accessible.

questions.q: What is the top level of the Unity Catalog three-level namespace?
options: The catalog
The metastore
The schema
The workspace
questions.explain: Catalogs sit directly below the metastore and are the first (top) level of the catalog.schema.table namespace.

questions.q: Which four main object types live inside a Unity Catalog schema?
options: Tables, views, volumes, and functions (including registered models)
Only tables and views â€” volumes and models belong to the metastore directly
Catalogs, schemas, workspaces, and metastores
Dashboards, notebooks, jobs, and clusters
questions.explain: A schema's children are tables, views, volumes, and functions â€” the last category including versioned, registered ML models.

questions.q: What single question determines whether a Unity Catalog table is managed or external?
options: Whether Unity Catalog picks the storage path, or you specify one yourself
Whether the table has a primary key defined
Whether the table was created with Python or SQL
Whether the table is in the workspace catalog or a custom catalog
questions.explain: A managed table's storage path is chosen and controlled by Unity Catalog; an external table's path is one you specify, already registered as an external location.

questions.q: What are the three kinds of principal Unity Catalog recognizes in a GRANT statement?
options: Users, groups, and service principals
Users, roles, and policies
Workspaces, catalogs, and schemas
Admins, editors, and viewers
questions.explain: A GRANT's TO clause always names a user, a group, or a service principal â€” the only three principal types Unity Catalog recognizes.

questions.q: What is the general syntax shape of a GRANT statement in Unity Catalog?
options: GRANT privilege_types ON securable_object TO principal
GRANT principal ON securable_object TO privilege_types
GRANT securable_object TO principal ON privilege_types
ALLOW privilege_types FOR principal ON securable_object
questions.explain: Unity Catalog's real GRANT syntax is GRANT privilege_types ON securable_object TO principal.

questions.q: By default, who owns a securable object when it's first created?
options: Whoever created it
The metastore admin, always
The account's root user
No one; ownership must be assigned manually before use
questions.explain: Every securable object has exactly one owner, defaulting to whoever created it, and owners automatically get all privileges on that object.

questions.q: Why is granting privileges to a group generally better than granting to individual users?
options: Onboarding and offboarding become a single group-membership change instead of separate GRANT/REVOKE pairs to track for each person
Groups run queries faster than individual users
Unity Catalog does not allow granting privileges to individual users at all
Group grants never need to be revoked
questions.explain: Granting to a group centralizes access management â€” adding or removing a person from the group handles access, instead of separate per-user grants accumulating as hard-to-audit exceptions.

questions.q: How does a row filter differ from a plain GRANT SELECT on a table?
options: A GRANT is all-or-nothing; a row filter is a UDF evaluated per row that excludes rows where it returns false
A row filter replaces GRANT entirely â€” tables with a row filter need no SELECT grant at all
A row filter only works on views, never on tables
A row filter is enforced only in notebooks, not in SQL warehouses
questions.explain: GRANT SELECT is binary (all rows or none). A row filter is a registered SQL function evaluated against every row at query time; rows where it returns false are silently excluded.

questions.q: What does a column mask function return, compared to a row filter function?
options: A value of the same type as the masked column, instead of a boolean
Always a boolean, exactly like a row filter
An integer error code
Nothing â€” masks don't use functions at all
questions.explain: A row filter returns true/false to include or exclude a row. A column mask returns a value of the masked column's type â€” the real value or a redacted substitute.

questions.q: What distinguishes a governed tag from an ordinary Unity Catalog tag?
options: A governed tag has a tag policy restricting its allowed values and who can assign it
A governed tag can only be applied to columns, never to tables
A governed tag is visible only to the user who created it
A governed tag automatically deletes the data it's attached to after 90 days
questions.explain: Governed tags add a tag policy: administrators define allowed values and control which users/groups can assign the tag, enforced consistently across the account.

questions.q: What does Databricks Data Classification do?
options: Uses an agentic AI system to scan Unity Catalog tables and automatically tag columns likely to contain sensitive data
Manually deletes any column containing PII
Encrypts every table in a catalog by default
Replaces the need for Unity Catalog grants entirely
questions.explain: Data Classification scans tables, detects sensitive data patterns (emails, SSNs, credit cards, etc.), and applies governed class.* tags to the matching columns.

questions.q: In a workspace enabled for Unity Catalog, what does navigational search review when you search for a table by text string?
options: Table names, table comments, column names, and column comments
Only the exact table name
Only the catalog and schema names
Only columns marked with a PII tag
questions.explain: Unity Catalog search looks at table names, table comments, column names, and column comments, so a well-described table is findable even with an obscure name.

questions.q: How does Unity Catalog capture data lineage?
options: Automatically, down to the column level, from queries run through Spark DataFrame or Databricks SQL interfaces
Only when a user manually draws a lineage diagram in Catalog Explorer
Only for tables explicitly tagged 'lineage-tracked'
Only for data ingested through Delta Live Tables
questions.explain: Lineage is captured automatically from real query activity against Unity Catalog tables â€” no manual diagramming or tagging is required.

questions.q: Which column should you filter on for query performance when querying system.access.audit, per Databricks' own recommendation?
options: event_date
event_time
request_id
session_id
questions.explain: Databricks recommends filtering on event_date (a date column) rather than event_time (a timestamp), because the table's performance optimizations are built around event_date.

questions.q: What does Lakehouse Monitoring add on top of row filters, column masks, and audit logs?
options: It profiles a table on a schedule and generates a dashboard, showing whether data quality and access patterns hold up over time
It replaces the need for Unity Catalog grants entirely
It automatically deletes tables that fail a quality check
It is only used for billing, not data quality
questions.explain: Monitoring answers whether the controls set up elsewhere are still working over time â€” row filters and masks set the rule, monitoring checks the ongoing result.

questions.q: In Unity Catalog, what kind of object is a Delta share?
options: A static file export with no further governance
A securable object â€” owned, permissioned, and auditable like a catalog or table
A temporary cache that expires after 24 hours
A copy of the data stored outside Unity Catalog entirely
questions.explain: A share is itself a Unity Catalog securable object, with an owner and its own grants â€” Delta Sharing extends the governance model rather than bypassing it.

questions.q: What namespace does a registered model use in Unity Catalog?
options: A flat, single-part model ID with no catalog or schema
The same three-level catalog.schema.model namespace tables use
A separate 'models' namespace unrelated to catalogs and schemas
The Databricks workspace ID followed by a run ID
questions.explain: Registered models use the exact same catalog.schema.model three-level namespace as tables, which is what lets them inherit the same owners, permissions, and audit trail as any other object in that schema.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four documented paths for migrating a Hive metastore table to Unity Catalog?
options: Upgrade wizard + SYNC
CLONE
CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT (CTAS)
DELETE FROM hive_metastore and manually re-upload the files
questions.explain: The four real paths are the upgrade wizard/SYNC, CLONE, CTAS, and UCX for workspace-scale automation â€” manually deleting and re-uploading isn't a documented migration path.

questions.q: In the Driftwood Trail Outfitters scenario, what replaces the three separate per-workspace Hive metastores?
options: Three separate Unity Catalog metastores, one per region
A single Unity Catalog metastore with all three workspaces attached
A shared spreadsheet listing all tables
Nothing â€” the Hive metastores stay as they were
questions.explain: Chapter 1's fix is one Unity Catalog metastore replacing three independent Hive metastores, giving the whole organization one governed boundary instead of three.
